newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week - turbulent ahead of budget.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week - turbulent ahead of budget.

text.p: UK gilts face a turbulent week as they await Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's first budget on July 2 and lack any significant economic data to occupy them in the meantime, analysts said on Monday.
"There is not an awful lot of data to get our teeth into this week in the sterling market," said London Bond Broking analyst Andrew Davies.
"In the background, of course, we have concerns over the shape of the budget coming up next week. That will feature a lot in people's thinking."
The gilts market will pounce on any clue as to how much Brown is likely to tighten the government purse strings in the budget as it will have a direct baring on the interest rate outlook.

"If this budget comes out quite tight that could release some pressures (on UK interest rates) and might suggest we do not need as many hikes on interest rates," said CIBC Wood Gundy economist Audrey Child-Freeman.
"We should remain in some sort of uncertain and worried territory at least until the budget."
The only UK economic data this week are trade figures on Wednesday and final first quarter GDP figures on Friday. Neither will offer much inspiration, analysts said.

Gilts and short sterling took a battering on Monday, following speculation in weekend newspapers that the Bank of England would tighten interest rates by more than financial markets had been expecting.
Gilts sold off early on and stood at 113-01 in Monday's afternoon trade, down 15/32 on the day.

The September short sterling contract stood at 92.97, just about discounting a half-point rate rise by the end of the third quarter. Last Monday, it was factoring in only a quarter point rise in the period.
But Monday's sharp sell may be the main move of the week, said GNI analysts Mark Henry.
"Gilts might lick their wounds and hover around these levels and wait for the budget," Henry said. "It's going to be a case of treading water."
The market reaction was a measure of the lack of data to act on, Henry said.
Analysts said the September gilt future would hover within a range of 112-25 on the downside and 113-25 on the top.
Wednesday sees the auction of two billion sterling in 10-year gilts, but analysts said the sale was not likely to suffer from the ongoing volatility and cover of two times was likely.

Financial market turbulence is not likely to end with the July 2 budget as the Bank of England's monetary policy committee meets a week later on July 9 and 10. Many economists forecast a rate rise will follow meeting.

Spending has been bolstered by the return of high consumer confidence or the "feel-good factor", rising employment and an accelerating real earnings growth, investment bank Merrill Lynch said in a client note.
Sizeable windfall gains from recent flotation of building societies and insurance companies such as Halifax, Alliance and Leicester and Norwich Union may also prove inflationary, it added.
Davies said the problem with the UK economy was one of balance between the export sector, which is straining under the strength of sterling, and a burgeoning domestic sector, particularly services.
"The more money he can take out of the economy in the budget the better he will be able to improve the balance between the domestic and the international sectors," Davies said.
He added that trading volumes in gilts were likely to be sluggish this week given that it was the end of the month, quarter and half-year.
"People are unlikely to do anything particularly aggressive and they may even book one or two profits," he said.
